They will administer locals prior to a procedure (for example, prior to suturing a laceration) but there is little point in administering them for localized pain relief for pain that is already in progress because their duration of action is so short. In addition, your body's reaction to bacteria creates an acidic environment that limits the utility of local anesthetics to work properly. I would also say that very few physicians are actually adequately trained in issues pertaining to teeth and the oral cavity because that is usually left to dentists. Yes and no. The problem isn't access to insurance. I actually have decent insurance via my job, probably better than anything I'd get via signing up on my own. The problem is evil insurance companies using any under handed tactic they can dream up to avoid making payments. Pre obamacare one of the most common tactic was the idea of "pre existing condition". It was the bane of my existence, I've passed on really good job offers for fear of getting seriously I'll during the 3-6 month period in which a new insurance carrier would refuse to pay for any medical treatment.

Obamacare explicitly made the "pre existing condition" excuse illegal. So that's a big improvement. But it doesn't completely solve the problem as insurance companies still find ridiculous reasons to justify avoiding making payments.

To be fair, it isn't completely free. If you are a dependent (under age of majority) or otherwise earn under I think 30k~/year, you pay nothing at all. Over that threeshold though, and you pay something like $70/month into the healthcare, but it covers pretty well whatever happens inside a hospital. Drugs are subsidized, but certainly not free. Same for cost of living if you are in long term care for something nasty. I have a friend who's wife is now going through round-two of cancer, and the first round cost them over 70k I think in travel back-and-forth (we live on an island and ferry's cost $78 for car and one person, one direction, plus gas and food for the 4 hours of driving but a few times every week), accommodations, misc meds etc.

But the idea that a twisted ankle will bankrupt you is totally nonexistent here. You can also do things like oral surgery through a hospital if you don't want to pay for a private surgeon, you just have to wait longer for it. I've cut my leg open with a ski, and cut my finger along with some chicken. I don't have pics of a surgery I had when I was two, or that toenail I ripped off, but that was all covered as well. You walk in, show them what's up, give them your health number, they triage you based on severity and then off you go. Walk out a while later, potentially with a prescription. All imaging and testing is covered, lab work, fluids, meds and bed time. Same for a basic medial clinic or doctor visit.

It's not perfect, if you're senior citizen that needs a hip replaced, you're on a long-ass wait-list or some other "non-emergency" type of procedure, you're waiting for a good while.

the pleasure of speaking about imaginary things
Why do we like to speak about imaginary things?

I think we like to speak about imaginary things because it gets us out of our tiny little reality. Humans need to get out of their lives and bodies, and there are many ways to do that; one of them is to let our wild imagination speak.
Still, no excuse to spend tithe money on stuffy celibate fellows debating how many angels can dance on the head of a pin.
I'm sorry what? Were the angels mentioned in the article or what? I'm confused.

It was a topic of debate amongst scholars in the dark ages. Thomas Aquinas could apparently discuss and write at great length over the minutiae of most Christian myths, such as how many angels could stand on the head of a pin or whether the inhabitants of Heaven needed to defecate.
It can be a way to look at our current reality in an abstract manner. If everything is hypothetical, it's easier to brainstorm/spitball theories without fear of judgment.

I think one reason is because whether we know it or not we question ourselves about choices we have made in life and especially in those cases where its not consciously known, it comes out in the form of imagination. It allows us to form ideas about what might have been and make justification about why we didn't choose that path over the one taken. Speaking it out as an idea helps to reinforce your mindset since most people only speak about imaginary things with people who are likely to agree with them like friends or close family.
I believe, it is because the abstract is the most difficult to describe.
Imagination, not necessity, is the mother of all inventions.
Because we frequently benefit from using symbols as stand-ins for more complex concepts.
A work of fiction can often draw a particular idea into sharp focus, when all the historical instances that actually dealt with the same idea have so many variables that it muddies the waters.
